3664.dq: Dza is a tonal language and tone plays a function in lexical and grammatical contrast. So far, three contrastive level tonesː H, M and L are clearly attested. [Othaniel 2020: 29] (The lexical contrasts are on monosyllabic citation forms in Table 3.10, i.e. word-level tone; the grammatical tones are floating tones on the sentence-final TBU. No stress of any domain is described.)
3664.dloc: Othaniel 2020: ch. 3 Phonology and orthography, §3.1.3 Lexical and Grammatical Tone, p. 29; §3.1.5 Syllable Structure, p. 34; §3.2.3 Tone, p. 38. Othaniel 2022: §3.4.4 Syllable types and word structures in Dza, p. 21.
3664.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Dza is described as a tone language with three contrastive level tones (H, M, L) and three contour tones (HL, LH, LHL); tone carries lexical contrasts (minimal sets in Table 3.10) and grammatical contrasts (interrogative vs declarative mood by a floating falling tone on the sentence-final TBU, object vs possessive pronoun, habitual negation, locative nominals). Vowel length is non-contrastive; words are typically monosyllabic, nouns up to four syllables. The words stress and accent (prosodic sense) do not occur in any of the nine saved descriptions.

3664.idn: Dza (Jenjo, Jen), the present-day 'unified dialect' of Dza town; data: Dza (Jen) town, Karim-Lamido LGA, Taraba State, Nigeria; texts from fieldwork 2015/2016 and December 2018 - February 2019; eight consultants aged 32-78 from Dza town
3664.tone: Tone system: three level tones H, M, L plus contours HL, LH, LHL (Othaniel 2020: 29; repeated in Othaniel 2022: 19 'adapted from Othaniel 2020'); Benson 2020 (Ideophones, LiA 1(3): 341) gives 'three primary tone levels and contours involving all three levels' and disyllabic melodies. Every syllable has a TBU (vowel or syllabic nasal). The sources do not discuss stress: neither 'stress' nor 'accent' in the prosodic sense appears anywhere (the only hits are 'acute accent'/'circumflex accent' as orthographic tone diacritics in Othaniel 2020 §3.2.3, acoustic 'prominence' (CPP, harmonics) in Othaniel 2022, and 'prominent' in the sociolinguistic sense). No source denies stress either, so this is a tone description with no stress rule, not an explicit no-stress claim.

3666.dloc: Wallace 1969, sec. 3 'Word Structure and phoneme Distribution', p. 69.
3666.prule: Stress ('the major stress') always on the main syllable, which is the last syllable of the word: the Katu word is (c₃v)(c₂v)(c₁v) + MS, zero to three presyllables (vowel /a/, usually an unstressed [ə]) before a single full main syllable (C₁V±C₄ or C₂C₃V±C₄). Hence final stress in every 2-4 syllable word; monosyllables are the main syllable.
3666.srule: None: 'Presyllables are always unstressed.' (one stress per word, on the word-final main syllable; Wallace 1969 pp. 69-71 mentions no secondary or minor stress).
3666.quote: The katu word has a main syllable which can be precedeŋ by one, two, or three presyllables. The word can be symbolized as c₃v/c₂v/c₁v/ MS. 3667.dq: Den exspiratoriska huvudaksenten hvilar i allmänhet på ordets första betonade stavelse (Vendell 1904 § 40, p. XXV). Sentence-position effects are treated separately: 'Sammalunda va i satserna: jér va he; he va jer' (Vendell 1892 § 14.3b, p. 198); 'vissa enstafviga ord, då de genom sin ställning i satsen förlora tonvikten' (Freudenthal 1889 § 10.11).
3667.dloc: Inledning, Kap. III 'Aksent', § 40, pp. XXV–XXVI (pp. 31–32 of the archive.org copy ordbokverdestsv00vendgoog)
3667.prule: Expiratory main stress (fortis) falls 'i allmänhet' (in general) on the first stress-bearing syllable of the word throughout the East Swedish (Finland-Swedish) folk dialects (Vendell 1904 § 40); Ostrobothnian dialects keep initial stress even where the ultima/penultima has a long vowel, i.e. also in loanwords (Vendell 1904 § 40 p. XXVI; Freudenthal 1878 § 33 p. 57 'auch in ausländischen Lehnwörtern auf der ersten Sylbe ruht': Närpes predik, husér — Freudenthal's acute is a vowel-length mark, not a stress mark, p. 58; Ivars 2015:89–90 Karleby–Nedervetil 'kosin, 'ridzir, 'mosik). Regional deviation stated in the primary source: West Nyland (semifortis promoted to fortis; = Selenius 1972 'upptaktsbetoning' / Ivars 2015:285–286 'slutledsbetoning' in compounds with a monosyllabic first member: gräs'annd, sjö'bo:d, gås'ongi, smör'blommå), partly Hitis and Ålands härad (strengthened levis after acc. medius/compositus); Ivars 2015:179 describes Åland as having 'den för svenskan normala rörliga betoningen' ('strömming, 'tjä:reld but ak'sjo:n, för'äldrar, his'torja, per'fekt).
3667.srule: Pedersöre-Purmo (N Ostrobothnia), Vendell 1892 § 14.2–3: strong secondary stress ('stark biton') on the first syllable of a trisyllable whose final syllable carries main stress (briŋgarí) and on a long or closed first syllable of a compound's second member (bötstam); weak secondary stress ('svag biton') on a short open first syllable of a second member after a long monosyllabic first member, on the second syllable of a disyllable with initial main stress (tuta 'tålig') and on the third syllable of a tri- or polysyllable with initial main stress (flikunå 'flickorna'); every syllable between two stressed syllables is unstressed. The language-wide source (Vendell 1904 § 40) names the grades semifortis/levis only to note their regional strengthening in compounds (West Nyland semifortis > fortis; Hitis, Ålands härad strong levis) and gives no placement; in West Nyland trisyllables the secondary (second tone peak) sits on the second syllable, not the third (Selenius 1972 § 5.4, pp. 112–122).

3679.dq: all syllables in any Penan sentence are pronounced with an even, equal stress.

3680.dq: Basically, the system is one of quantity sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge of the word, i.e., a preferred rhythm of weak-strong, in which the weak position may only be filled by a short vowel. The final syllable is often analyzed as extrametrical.
3680.heavy: Long-vowel syllable: 'the weak position may only be filled by a short vowel', i.e. a long vowel can only be a foot head (strong). Coda consonants are not mentioned as weight-bearing.
3680.dflt: In a word of short vowels only, feet are built weak-strong from the left, so the even-numbered syllables (second, fourth...) are strong and the odd-numbered ones weak (and syncopate in the southeastern dialects); the final syllable is treated as extrametrical. Not stated as a separate default by the source; this follows from the iambic left-edge rule.
3680.prule: Quantity-sensitive iambic feet built left-to-right from the left edge of the word (weak-strong); the weak position of a foot may only be a short-vowel syllable, so every long-vowel syllable is a foot head (strong/stressed) and in a run of short vowels the even-numbered syllable from the left is strong; the final syllable is 'often analyzed as extrametrical'. Which foot head carries primary word stress is NOT stated in this source (for the Odawa half of the same cluster, Kaye 1973 / Piggott 1980, 1983 as restated in Newell & Piggott 2006:282-283 and Swierzbin 2003:355: antepenultimate stressed vowel in words with three or more stressed vowels, otherwise the penultimate stressed vowel).
3680.srule: Valentine 1996 locates all stresses but does not rank them as primary vs secondary: quantity-sensitive iambic feet are parsed left to right from the word's left edge, so every long-vowel syllable and every even-numbered syllable in a run of short-vowel syllables is strong (stressed) and the odd-numbered short-vowel syllables are weak (unstressed; syncopated in the southeastern dialects); the final syllable is 'often analyzed as extrametrical'. No statement of which strong syllable is the main stress (see Primary stress for the Odawa-literature loci).
3680.quote: STRESS. The stress system of Ojibwe has been analyzed by a number of researchers (Bloomfield 1958, Rhodes 1976, Valentine 1985, etc.). Basically, the system is one of quantity sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge of the word, i.e., a preferred rhythm of weak-strong, in which the weak position may only be filled by a short vowel. The final syllable is often analyzed as extrametrical. Very similar stress systems have been proposed for other Algonquian languages, e.g., Passamaquoddy (Stowell 1979). In southeastern dialects of Ojibwe, a very prominent rule of weak vowel syncope is resul…
3680.idn: Valentine 1996 states the stress rule for Ojibwe as a whole (all dialects); Eastern Ojibwa is covered as one of the 'southeastern dialects of Ojibwe' with weak-vowel syncope (his sources include Rhodes 1985 for Ottawa-Eastern Ojibwa-Chippewa), and no rule specific to this language alone is given.
3680.exq_: Some dialects show clear evidence of stress shifts, as well, particularly with words that consist only of short vowels. ... Some dialects, notably those in northern Ontario, show stress shifts in sequences of short vowels. I have marked the stress on syllables as documented with a Severn Ojibwe spe…
3680.tone: Not a tone language. Valentine 1996 p. 312: in northern dialects such as Berens River 'the correlate of stress in these dialects is pitch'; for the Eastern Ojibwa-Odawa cluster Rhodes 1976 (Algonquian Papers 7, p. 155 fn.) says of Kaye 1973 that 'he calls it stress rather than the pitch or pitch accent which it is'; SPA 1979 entry 735 (reading Bloomfield 1957 p. 3) reports 'two pitch-stress patterns' in phrase-final and sentence-final position; an Open Library excerpt of Harms 1968 (exercise on Bloomfield's data) says words of three or more syllables carry high pitch on the second syllable, disyllables on the first (grade excerpt, not used for the verdict).

evidence_works.work: Bowers 2019, The Nishnaabemwin restructuring controversy: new empirical evidence (Phonology 36: 187-224)
evidence_works.detail: The stress rule in Bowers 2019 is restated, not measured: 'the uncontroversial iambic stress pattern common in Ojibwe dialects (Valentine 1994)... the typical Ojibwe dialect has iteratively assigned left-aligned iambs, with otherwise unparseable final syllables placed in a degenerate foot. While syllables with long vowels are always heavy, closed syllables are not'. Its first-hand content is a judgment study, not an instrumental one: 20 native speakers of the Odawa variety (Manitoulin Island 15, Walpole Island 5), ages 61-87, judged 1,441 words drawn randomly from Corbiere & Valentine 2016, presented in roman orthography; survey 1 = ratings and forced choice among prefix allomorphs on non-alternating stems, survey 2 = forced choice between 1930s alternating prefixed forms and modern leveled forms, survey 3 = forced choice between 1930s forms and unattested foils. Nothing acoustic was measured and stress placement was not probed; fn. 1 states that stress is marked only for 1930s forms 'since with the loss of unstressed syllables, there is no prominence contrast between unstressed and secondarily stressed syllables'. Result: the cohort born in and after the 1930s prefers innovative prefixes and leveled paradigms while still recognising the 1930s forms, so Bowers argues that modern Nishnaabemwin has no synchronic rhythmic syncope (sec. 7). This corroborates and dates the 'restructuring of much of the lexicon and the form of inflectional person prefixes' that the entry's Valentine 1996 quote reports for the southeastern dialects.

3681.prule: No positional rule: accent is lexically fixed per stem ('a basic accent on a certain syllable' that 'tends to remain on that syllable throughout inflexion'), with frequent token-to-token variation in Speck's transcriptions; certain noun-inflection suffixes (-m-, -ǝnaw-, -owy-) pull the accent onto the preceding syllable; verb-stem accents 'if there are any, are too uncertain to be indicated' (p. 64-65).

3682.prule: Fixed final: every word is pronounced with greatest force on its last syllable, which is also the only syllable bearing the full tonal contrasts (pretonic syllables take only high 2 or low 4). Weight plays no role. Native words are mono- or disyllabic; trisyllabic compounds and Spanish loans of more than two syllables are pronounced as a two-word phrase (minor word + principal word), each part final-stressed, with 'un poco del acento original' remaining on the first syllable of a compound.
3682.srule: None in native (mono-/disyllabic) words: non-final syllables are 'pretónicas' (p. 352). Only in compounds and long loans: trisyllabic compounds keep 'un poco del acento original' on the first syllable and are pronounced 'como si fuera una frase que consta de dos palabras' (jakatunʔ 'tamal' < tyaja + katunʔ), main stress still final; Spanish loans of more than two syllables are likewise split into two parts when pronounced (p. 348).

3682.tone: Tonal language with fixed final stress: two level tones (2 high, 4 low) plus six glides (43, 32, 21 rising; 12, 23, 45 falling) contrast on the final = stressed syllable (kala² 'tejido' / kala²¹ 'ponerse tieso' / kala²³ 'milpa tierna' / kala³² 'juntar' / kala⁴ 'llegar' / kala⁴³ / kala⁴⁵); pretonic syllables carry only 2 or 4, generally opposite to the following tone, and 2-2 / 4-4 disyllables are rare and never level. Tense and person are partly marked by tone changes on the root (sec. 2.2). Stress is not conditioned by tone; the orthographic 'acento' marks the higher-toned member of a homograph pair, not stress placement.

3687.dq: The general pattern for words in isolation is /LˈH/ (iambic) or—for nominalized verbs with lexical prefixes—/LLˈH/ (anapestic).
3687.dloc: Section 'Stress and Weight' in the PHONOLOGY chapter, ms. pp. 14-15: heading, first paragraph and footnotes 6-7 on p. 14; continuation with examples (1)-(2) and the compound sentence on p. 15. Supporting: PHONOLOGY opening, ms. p. 13 'a confounded system of final stress and vowel length'; Tones, ms. pp. 15-16 (three tones, HL only on stressed syllables); Table 16 and the paragraph after it, ms. p. 22; vowel-formant discussion, ms. p. 10 (unstressed 'minor' prefix syllables transcribed [ə]).
3687.heavy: The source invokes weight ('Roots are simply long (bimoraic) and stressed while prefixes are short (monomoraic) and unstressed') but defines heavy = root and light = affix/particle; there are 'no stress or weight alternations', and no segmental definition of a bimoraic syllable independent of root status is given (the syllable template C1(C2)(C3)V1(V2)(N) applies to roots and prefixes alike). Weight is therefore a correlate of morpheme class, not an independent conditioning factor.
3687.prule: Stress is non-contrastive and falls on the root morpheme's syllable: roots are the only long (bimoraic) syllables and are stressed; prefixes (nominalizer, lexical prefix, nasal prefix), suffixes and particles are short (monomoraic) and unstressed. Since native morphemes are monosyllabic and the root closes a simple word, isolation forms are iambic /LˈH/ (prefix + root) or anapestic /LLˈH/ (two prefixes + root); compounds carry one stress per root, with no restriction on adjacent stressed syllables. The authors state weight and morphology are confounded, so the same rule can be phrased as 'stress the bimoraic syllable'.
3687.srule: No secondary stress described: a simple word has one stressed syllable, the root (/LˈH/ prefix+root, /LLˈH/ two prefixes+root; all affixes and particles unstressed). Only compounds carry more than one stress, one per root, adjacent stresses allowed ('There is no restriction on having multiple stressed syllables (roots) occur contiguously. This is actually quite common in (compound) nouns and verbs'); no primary/secondary ranking among them is given.
3687.quote: East Tusom, like other Tangkhulic languages, has non-contrastive stress that is predictable from weight and morphological factors (which are confounded). There are no stress or weight alternations in our data (but two short syllables sometimes coalesce to form a long syllable). Except in loanwords, morphemes are all monosyllabic (or occasionally, subsyllabic). Roots are simply long (bimoraic) and stressed while prefixes are short (monomoraic) and unstressed. tn.quote: Tone in Ebira functions at two distinct levels. It functions at the lexical level and at the grammatical level. ... Tone is symbolised as follows: High tone - H - marked ´ Mid tone - M - unmarked Low tone - L - marked ` High-Falling tone - HF - marked ˆ Low-Rising tone - LR - marked ˇ Down Step - H' - marked Automatic tone downstep occurs only under specific tone contractions of HLH → H'H (see 3.4.5). It can be observed from the above that Ebira has three level tones and two kinetic tones. ... Every syllable has a tonal feature as one of its phonological components.

3689.dq: Per the near-identical distribution of tones across these different syllable shapes, I take the tone-bearing unit in Atchan to be the syllable, rather than a smaller unit like the mora. (Tone is described on roots, words and phrases; no word-level stress domain is discussed.)
3689.dloc: Ch. 3 'The phonology of Atchan', §3.4 Tone, p. 65; §3.4.1.1 Nouns, p. 66; §3.5 Discussion, p. 86.
3689.prule: No word-stress rule stated. Two underlying tones /L/ and /H/, tone-bearing unit = syllable; lexical melodies on monosyllabic noun roots /L/, /H/, /LH/, /HL/ (plus /L HL/ on disyllabic noun roots); verb roots /L/ or /H/; grammatical tone by overlay and polarity; surface levels H, M, L, SuperLow and five falling contours from spreading, plateauing and depressor consonants. Stress, accent and metrical prominence are never mentioned for Atchan.
3689.quote: Atchan makes use of two contrastive tones – Low (L) and High (H). Four distinct tone levels – High, Mid, Low, and SuperLow – and five contours – High-Low, High-Mid, Mid-Low, Low-SuperLow, and SuperLow-even lower – appear on the surface, all of which are attributable to the interaction of the two underlying tones and a number of regular tonal processes like High-tone spreading and plateauing (Lojenga, 1985; Bôle-Richard, 2008; Russell, 2023). 3689.idn: Atchan (the language 'commonly known by the name Ebrié'), spoken by the Tchaman in and around Abidjan; author's own corpus, collected mainly in the villages Anono and Blockhauss (ÁnOnkwathé), both neighborhoods of Abidjan; data: Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire: six in-person field trips…
3689.tone: The source describes Atchan as a two-tone language (underlying L and H, syllable = TBU) with lexical and grammatical tone (overlay, polarity, High-tone spreading, plateauing, depressor consonants). In the 321-page text 'stress(ed)' occurs only for Paraguayan Guaraní and in two bibliography titles; 'accent' only in fn. 12 naming the tone diacritics; 'foot' as a prosodic level only in the Ch. 1 typological table of nasal-harmony domains, where it is the domain for Mwan and Ngen, not Atchan, and in one general theoretical sentence; 'prominent' is defined morphosyntactically in Ch. 5 ('I use the term prominent here to refer to morphosyntactic contexts in which the noun is not structurally dependent on another nominal head') though the phrase 'prosodically prominent positions' appears twice about noun class prefix obligatoriness, not about stress. No statement of word stress, accent or metrical structure for Atchan anywhere.

3690.dq: This is not to assert that there is no stress at all in Efik or the other LC languages. There is likely some sort phrasal stress, and also the juncture between elements of compound words appears to be marked by stress, but these are clearly not what Ward was referring to. [Connell 1994 p. 10] From a lexical standpoint, the tone systems found in the Lower Cross languages are relatively straightfor…
3690.dloc: Connell 1991: sec. 2.2.2 p. 47; sec. 2.3.3.3 pp. 54-55 and fn. 32 p. 55; fn. 34 p. 56; Ebughu in the sample p. 5; field-data caveat p. 14; Ibibio stress remark p. 104. Connell 1994: sec. 3.3 p. 10 (scan); sec. 5 p. 12 (scan).
3690.prule: No word-stress rule. Ebughu, as one of the 19 Lower Cross languages of Connell's sample, is a two-tone (H, L) terraced-level tone language with contrastive downstep and falling (less often rising) contours; Connell 1994 p. 10 names Ebughu among the languages where falling tones are common, from H-L-H tone spreading. Connell finds no true evidence for word-level (verb-stem) stress in Efik or the other LC languages (1991 p. 55 and fn. 32) and, in the same discussion of Cook's Efik syllabeme, calls the language under analysis 'a non-stress language' (fn. 34 p. 56, said of Efik, the LC language treated there); he allows only 'likely some sort phrasal stress' and stress marking compound junctures.

3690.idn: Group-level basis: Connell 1991 treats the Lower Cross group with Ebughu as one of 19 sample languages (p. 5; 1988 field data, 'detailed cross-checking was not possible', p. 14); the tone characterization is stated for all LC languages (1991 p. 47; 1994 p. 10 names Ebughu), while the stress remarks concern 'Efik or…
3690.tone: Two basic tones H and L on every LC language, plus phonologically significant (non-predictable) downstep; HL falling and, less often, LH rising contours on one syllable; terraced-level (Connell 1991 p. 47). Connell 1994 p. 10: 'Falling tones are common in some languages of the group, viz., Anaang (dialectally), Ebughu, Ibibio (dialectally), Ito, Itu Mbon Uso, Nkari, and Usaghade, where they are a result of tone spreading (H L H HL)'; p. 12: 'Tonal systems in the group appear to be further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done.' On stress: word-level stress in Ward's (1933) verb-stem sense rejected for lack of evidence (1991 p. 55); phrasal stress and compound-juncture stress conjectured for 'Efik or the other LC languages' (fn. 32); 'a non-stress language' (fn. 34, p. 56) is said in the Efik syllabeme discussion, so it is Efik-anchored and extends to the group only via fn. 32; p. 104 (not 103) says consonant weakening 'may be related to stress in Ibibio, an area of Ibibio phonology which to date remains unstudied.'
